metadata.narrative: We’re a small HR-tech company that uses AI to screen resumes, rank candidates, and generate interview questions. We currently sell in the U.S. but are considering pilots in the EU, UK, Canada, Singapore, Australia, and maybe China. What should we keep in mind before expanding? I’m especially worried about whether hiring AI is treated as high risk, what notices or audits we may need, how the U.S. differs from the EU, and whether we should build one global compliance program or separate regional versions.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Whether hiring AI is treated as "high risk" depends entirely on which market you're in, ranging from an emphatic yes to an explicit no.

In the EU, AI systems used for recruitment or candidate selection, screening applications, evaluating candidates, or monitoring worker performance are named directly in Annex III of the AI Act as high-risk, triggering the Act's heaviest compliance tier for both developers and deploying employers.

The EU AI Act also reaches outside the EU, applying to providers or users anywhere whose AI output is used within the Union, with penalties up to the higher of €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover.
In the US there is no single federal high-risk designation; instead a patchwork of tools does similar work.

The EEOC's Title VII guidance frames the issue as disparate-impact risk via the "four-fifths rule" (a selection rate below 80% of the highest group's rate is evidence of adverse impact), and the EEOC and DOJ separately warn that AI screening can violate the ADA by failing to accommodate disabilities or screening out disabled candidates through proxies like speech patterns.
The White House's Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights and NIST's voluntary AI Risk Management Framework add non-binding expectations around notice and explanation, but carry no force of law.

Colorado's AI Act, effective February 2026, is the first US state law to formally define "high-risk AI systems" for consequential decisions including employment, imposing duty-of-care, impact-assessment, and consumer notice/explanation/appeal obligations, with a carve-out for businesses of 50 or fewer employees.

New York City's Local Law 144 skips "high risk" language, instead singling out "automated employment decision tools" for annual independent bias audits with published impact-ratio results and advance candidate notice.

A Cornell-led study found compliance thin — only 18 published audits and 11 notices across roughly 400 employers reviewed — partly because the law lets employers self-determine whether it applies to them.

Illinois has required disclosure and consent for AI-analyzed video interviews since 2019, and the EEOC has already settled an age-discrimination case (EEOC v. iTutorGroup) over a tool that filtered out older applicants.

The UK sits closer to the US than the EU on formal classification: it has deliberately declined to legislate, relying on the Equality Act 2010 and UK GDPR, while issuing non-statutory "Responsible AI in Recruitment" guidance recommending impact assessments, bias audits, and applicant signposting.

A UK parliamentary report has even recommended removing GDPR Article 22 (the EU's core automated-decision-making right) from UK law, and UK guidance flags an unresolved question of whether liability for a discriminatory vendor tool falls on employer or supplier.

Canada's federal AIDA would impose EU-style obligations, requiring impact assessments for "high-impact" systems, published explanations of intended and actual use, and penalties up to the higher of C$25 million or 5% of global revenue, with extraterritorial reach over international and interprovincial trade.
Ontario's Working for Workers legislation separately makes it the first Canadian jurisdiction to mandate employer disclosure of AI use in hiring directly to applicants.
Singapore and Australia both currently decline to treat hiring AI as legally high-risk.

Singapore's government states plainly it has no AI-specific law and no immediate plans for one, relying instead on existing fair-employment rules and the voluntary Model AI Governance Framework, reasoning that bias "with or without AI" is already covered.

Australia likewise has no law governing AI recruitment tools, only a voluntary AI Ethics Framework and no requirement to tell candidates AI is screening them, a gap a lawyer attributes to low public understanding and heavy unmonitored vendor reliance, illustrated by Services Australia having 11 promotions overturned for lacking human review.
For China, I could not find a hiring-specific AI regulation comparable to the EU's Annex III or NYC's audit regime.

On notices and audits generally, expect at minimum: pre-use disclosure to candidates (NYC, Colorado, Ontario, EU, UK all converge here), a periodic independent bias/impact audit, a retained documented impact assessment, and a channel for candidates to request human review, echoing GDPR Article 22's right to human intervention, which Recital 71 ties explicitly to "e-recruiting practices without any human intervention."

On the EU-versus-US question, the structural difference is that the EU pre-classifies your product category as high-risk by statute before deployment, while the US determines risk after the fact through disparate-impact litigation and an uneven set of state laws; the UK and Canada sit in between, the UK closer to the US's reactive model and Canada closer to the EU's ex-ante model.
On one global program versus separate regional ones, the evidence points toward a hybrid.

ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI RMF are increasingly cited across EU, US, Canadian, Australian, and Brazilian materials as a common technical backbone for an AI management system, and Canadian counsel explicitly recommends multinational companies build "a co-ordinated global compliance program" given that both the EU AI Act and Canada's AIDA reach extraterritorially.

Practically, that suggests one internal core — bias testing, documentation, human-review workflow, vendor accountability — aligned to the strictest applicable standard (today, the EU AI Act's Annex III regime), with thin jurisdiction-specific modules layered on top for each market's distinct notice format, audit cadence, and disclosure language: NYC's published impact ratios, Colorado's plain-language multilingual notice, Ontario's hiring-disclosure requirement, and the UK's Equality Act-driven reasonable-adjustments process.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Answer what was actually asked,
grounded in what you find with your search tools. Prior knowledge may help you
choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

Match your effort to the question. A narrow factual question deserves a couple
of searches and a couple of sentences; a broad, multi-part request deserves
sustained research and a full report. Answering a simple question at length
does not make the answer better — it makes it worse, and it wastes the
reader's time. Let the request set the size of both the search and the answer.

The request sets the kind of answer too, not just its size. A request to make
something wants that thing actually built, carrying the voice, structure, and
invention the brief implies — not a summary of what your sources say about it.
Some requests state that they want creativity; more often it is implicit, in a
task that cannot be done well without it or one dense enough that the work lies
in connecting things rather than listing them. When the request calls for that,
do the creative work: synthesise across your sources into something that is
yours, rather than restating each source in turn. Being evidence-grounded
constrains what you may assert, not how well you may write — every claim still
needs its support, but the shape, argument, and voice of the answer are yours
to build.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most useful reasonable reading — which for a
narrow question is a direct answer, not an expanded survey of the topic around
it. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed on the
strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally — briefly, and in proportion to
the request; a single factual question needs a moment's thought, not a plan:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Size the search to the question. When it has several independent coverage
   areas, begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across them.
   When it has one — a single fact, name, date, or definition — one or two
   queries is the whole search; if they answer it, stop and write.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- To keep anything from a batch, call `commit_context` on that turn. It may
  appear anywhere among the turn's actions; searches in the same turn always
  run after it.
- If you issue no `commit_context` on that turn, the batch is treated as your
  decision to keep none of it: every document is dropped and the turn's other
  actions still run. That is the correct move when nothing in the batch is
  worth keeping — but it is irreversible, so do not let a batch you wanted
  lapse by forgetting.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- Issue at most one `commit_context` per turn; several are ambiguous and lose
  the batch.
- New search calls may accompany `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If you cannot find support for a requested point,
say plainly in the report that you could not find it, rather than inventing an
answer — but say it in a searcher's voice, not in the vocabulary of this
section.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, give the best answer your
evidence permits and say plainly what you could not find.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers after the
  end of the supporting sentence, on the same line:
  `<the sentence, ending in its full stop.> [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Markers are stripped before the sentence is submitted, so they must sit
  outside its grammar: the sentence has to read correctly, and mean the same
  thing, once every marker is deleted.
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences) or JSON.
- Every line is a sentence of the report itself, read by someone who never saw
  this conversation and who receives these lines verbatim. Open on the first
  real sentence of the answer and close on its last. A line narrating your own
  process — what you are about to do, how the research went, what you conclude
  about your own conclusions — is not a report sentence and supports nothing.
- Write in your own voice, as the researcher. Every sentence asserts something
  about the subject the request asks about, and carries its markers. The
  markers do the attributing, so a sentence never announces that it is
  supported, nor what supports it, nor how far that support reaches.
- Exactly one kind of sentence may be about you rather than the subject: that
  you could not establish something. Say it once, plainly, in as few words as
  the point needs — no narrating the attempt, no restating it in other words,
  no explaining what left you unable. Everything else the reader receives is
  about the world, dated and specific, not about the answer's own provenance.
- Length follows the question, not the limit. Answer a narrow question in a
  sentence or two and stop; there is nothing to be gained by surrounding a
  one-line answer with background, and a reader who asked something simple
  will not read an essay. Only a genuinely broad, multi-part request should
  run long, and even then about 950 words is the practical ceiling: 1024 is a
  hard limit set by the evaluation and going over costs a full rewrite. Never
  pad toward a length.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

k.description: Number of fused passages to return (default 10).

tools.name: commit_context

documents.description: Evidence-worthy staged documents to retain. An empty array explicitly rejects the whole staged batch.

I now have solid, jurisdiction-specific evidence across the US, EU, UK, Canada, Singapore, and Australia, plus cross-cutting standards material. I have enough to write the full report.

Whether hiring AI is treated as "high risk" depends entirely on which market you're in, and the answer ranges from an emphatic yes to an explicit no.

In the EU, AI systems used for recruitment or candidate selection, screening applications, evaluating candidates, or monitoring worker performance are named directly in Annex III of the AI Act as high-risk, which triggers the Act's heaviest compliance tier for both developers and deploying employers.

Companies also need to know the EU AI Act reaches outside the EU: it applies to providers or users anywhere whose AI output is used within the Union, with penalties up to the higher of €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover.

In the US there is no single federal high-risk designation; instead a patchwork of tools does similar work.

The EEOC's 2021 Artificial Intelligence and Algorithmic Fairness Initiative and its later Title VII guidance frame the issue as disparate-impact risk, using the "four-fifths rule" (a selection rate for any protected group below 80% of the highest group's rate is treated as evidence of adverse impact), and the EEOC and DOJ have separately warned that AI screening tools can violate the ADA by failing to accommodate disabilities or by screening out disabled candidates through proxy signals like speech patterns or interview gaps. [shard_02907_42931] [shard_02072_44225] [shard_02613_31518]

The White House's 2022 Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights and NIST's voluntary AI Risk Management Framework add non-binding federal expectations around notice, explanation, and algorithmic-discrimination protections, but neither carries the force of law. [shard_02512_57481]

Colorado's AI Act, effective February 1, 2026, is the first comprehensive US state law to formally define "high-risk AI systems" for consequential decisions including employment, imposing duty-of-care, impact-assessment, and consumer notice/explanation/appeal obligations on developers and deployers (with a carve-out for businesses of 50 or fewer employees). [shard_01476_8852]

New York City's Local Law 144 does not use "high risk" language at all; it instead singles out "automated employment decision tools" for a narrower notice-and-audit regime: annual independent bias audits with published impact-ratio results, and advance notice to candidates with instructions for requesting an alternate process. [shard_02495_46894]

A Cornell-led study found real-world compliance thin, with only 18 published bias audits and 11 transparency notices found across roughly 400 employers reviewed, partly because the law lets employers self-determine whether it applies to them. [shard_00948_37956]

Illinois has separately required disclosure and consent for AI-analyzed video interviews since 2019, plus annual demographic reporting to the state if AI is the sole decision basis, and the EEOC has already settled an age-discrimination case (EEOC v. iTutorGroup) over an AI screening tool that filtered out older applicants. [shard_02072_44225]

The UK sits closer to the US than the EU on formal classification: its government has taken a deliberate "light touch" approach, declining to legislate and instead relying on the existing Equality Act 2010 and UK GDPR, while issuing non-statutory "Responsible AI in Recruitment" guidance recommending impact assessments, bias audits, and applicant signposting before and during deployment. [shard_02058_22956] [shard_01964_28928]

Notably, a UK parliamentary report has even recommended removing GDPR Article 22 (the EU's core automated-decision-making right) from UK law entirely, and the UK guidance flags an unresolved liability question: if a third-party AI vendor's tool discriminates, is it the employer or the vendor who bears the claim. [shard_05370_56971]

Canada's federal AIDA (part of Bill C-27) would impose EU-style obligations, requiring impact assessments for "high-impact" systems, published plain-language explanations of intended and actual use, and penalties up to the higher of C$25 million or 5% of global revenue for the most serious offences, and its scope over international/interprovincial trade means foreign employers doing business in Canada should consider themselves on notice. [shard_02318_43910] [shard_02805_52913]

Separately, Ontario's Working for Workers legislation makes it the first Canadian jurisdiction to mandate that employers disclose AI use in hiring directly to applicants, layering a provincial notice duty on top of the federal framework. [shard_04222_46386]

Singapore and Australia both currently decline to treat hiring AI as legally high-risk.

Singapore's government has stated plainly that it has no AI-specific law and no immediate plans for one, preferring to rely on existing fair-employment and workplace-fairness rules plus the voluntary Model AI Governance Framework and AI Verify testing toolkit, reasoning that bias "with or without AI" is already covered. [shard_02929_30608]

Australia likewise has no law governing AI recruitment tools, only a voluntary AI Ethics Framework, and no requirement to tell candidates that AI is screening them; a lawyer studying the space attributes this to low public understanding and heavy employer reliance on vendors without governance oversight, a gap illustrated by Services Australia having 11 promotions overturned after being made without human review. [shard_03967_79128]

For China, I could not find evidence of a hiring-specific AI regulation comparable to the EU Annex III or NYC's audit regime.

On notices and audits generally, expect at minimum: pre-use disclosure to candidates (NYC, Colorado, Ontario, EU, UK guidance all converge here), an independent bias/impact audit repeated periodically (annual under NYC and Colorado), a documented impact assessment retained for several years, and a channel for candidates to request human review or an alternate process (Colorado's right to appeal, GDPR Article 22's right to human intervention which Recital 71 explicitly ties to "e-recruiting practices without any human intervention"). [shard_06113_42519] [shard_01476_8852] [shard_02495_46894]

On your core EU-versus-US question, the structural difference is that the EU pre-classifies your product category as high-risk by statute before you ever deploy, while the US determines risk after the fact through disparate-impact litigation, agency guidance, and a growing but uneven set of state laws (Colorado, Illinois, New York City, with Colorado being the first true "high-risk" statute); the UK and Canada sit in between, the UK closer to the US's reactive model and Canada closer to the EU's ex-ante model.

On whether to build one global program or separate regional ones, your own evidence points toward a hybrid: ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI RMF are increasingly cited across EU, US, Canadian, Australian, and Brazilian materials as a common technical backbone for an AI management system (governance, risk assessment, documentation, monitoring), and Canadian counsel explicitly recommends multinational companies build "a co-ordinated global compliance program" given that both the EU AI Act and Canada's AIDA reach extraterritorially. [shard_01603_29704] [shard_00752_24408] [shard_02805_52913]

Practically, that suggests building one internal core (bias testing, documentation, human-review workflow, vendor accountability) aligned to the strictest applicable standard, which today is the EU AI Act's Annex III regime, and then layering thin, jurisdiction-specific modules on top for each market's distinct notice format, audit cadence, and disclosure language, such as NYC's published impact ratios, Colorado's plain-language multilingual notice, Ontario's hiring-disclosure requirement, and the UK's Equality Act-driven reasonable-adjustments process.
